item.title: C++ Concurrency and Parallel Programming (Part II)
item.description:
C++ Concurrency and Parallel Programming (Part II)

Author: Jingmengzhiyue()

This article is Part II of the C++ Concurrency and Parallel Programming series. Part I covered the execution model, thread lifecycles, mutexes, condition variables, and futures as a result channel; this installment continues with atomics and memory order, C++20’s cancellation and coordination facilities (stop_token, semaphore, latch, barrier), the engineering practices that take code from “correct” to “maintainable and measurable,” and finally a shutdown-capable concurrent task processor that computes squares.

To keep cross-references consistent, chapter and example numbering continues from Part I: this installment begins with Chapter 8 and Example 15, and references to Part I material are marked “Part I.”

item.title: C++ Concurrency and Parallel Programming (Part I)
item.description:
C++ Concurrency and Parallel Programming (Part I)

Author: Jingmengzhiyue()

Concurrent programs are hard to write not so much because of the sheer number of APIs, but because you must answer three questions clearly: Who owns the data, who may modify it, and what mechanism lets another thread use it safely? This article organizes C++ concurrency and parallel programming around those three questions. The code centers on the C++20 standard library and uses no third-party concurrency library.

This is Part I of the series. It covers, in order, the execution model, the build environment, thread lifecycles and argument passing, shared state and mutexes, multiple locks and deadlock, condition variables, and task result channels such as promise, packaged_task, and async. Part II goes on to discuss atomic variables and memory ordering, C++20’s cancellation and coordination facilities, engineering practice, and the implementation of a complete task processor.

OpenCV Basics

Author: Jingmengzhiyue()

This blog post covers the basics of OpenCV, a popular computer vision library. It explains how to load, display, and save images using OpenCV functions. Additionally, it delves into the Mat class, which is used to represent images in OpenCV as matrices. The post demonstrates how to create Mat objects, access their properties, and traverse and manipulate pixel values using both array-based and pointer-based methods.

#include <opencv2/opencv.hpp>
#include <iostream>
using namespace cv;
using namespace std;
int main(int argc, char** argv)
{
    cout << "start\n";
    // Read an image
    Mat src = imread("E:\\Datum\\Code\\CV4\\CV4\\a.png");
    if (src.empty()) {
        printf("could not open");
        return -1;
    }
    namedWindow("input", WINDOW_AUTOSIZE); // Create a window with the given title and automatic image size
    // In OpenCV 3, use namedWindow("input", CV_WINDOW_AUTOSIZE)
    imshow("input", src); // Display the image in the "input" window
    waitKey(0); // Prevent the window from closing immediately, wait for user input
    destroyAllWindows(); // Destroy all windows
    return 0;
}
  1. In OpenCV 4, you can directly use #include <opencv2/opencv.hpp> to import all OpenCV functions.
  2. using namespace cv; uses the OpenCV namespace.
  3. Define a Mat variable src and read an image into it.
  4. Perform robustness check; if the loaded image is not empty, display it.
  5. Use namedWindow("input", WINDOW_AUTOSIZE); to create a window. The first parameter is the window name, and the second parameter is the window size, which in OpenCV 4 is defined as automatic window size. In OpenCV 3, use nameWindow("input", CV_WINDOW_AUTOSIZE) to define the window.
  6. Use imshow("input", src) to display the image. The first parameter is the window to display in, and the second parameter is the image to display.
  7. To prevent the displayed image from disappearing immediately, use waitKey(0) to wait for user input.
  8. Use destroyAllWindows() to destroy all windows.

Python Fundamentals

Author: Jingmengzhiyue()

Prerequisites

I. Python Fundamentals

1. List Comprehensions and Conditional Assignment

When generating a sequence of numbers in Python, you can write it as follows:

1

L = []
def my_func(x):
    return 2*x
for i in range(5):
    L.append(my_func(i))
L

[0, 2, 4, 6, 8]

List comprehensions can actually simplify this notation: [* for i in *]. Here the first * is the mapping function, whose input is whatever i refers to in the latter part, whereas the second * denotes the object being iterated over.

C++ Core Programming

Author: Jingmengzhiyue()

C++ Core Programming

This stage offers a detailed treatment of C++ ==object-oriented== programming techniques, examining the core and essence of the language.

1 Memory Partition Model

When a C++ program runs, memory is broadly divided into 4 regions

  • Code segment: holds the binary code of function bodies and is managed by the operating system
  • Global segment: holds global variables, static variables, and constants
  • Stack segment: automatically allocated and freed by the compiler; it stores function parameters, local variables, and the like
  • Heap segment: allocated and freed by the programmer; if the programmer does not release it, the operating system reclaims it when the program ends
